text: Disinfectants are chemicals that kill pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi) on contact; products vary by concentration (e.g. 0.5%, 5%) and should be chosen based on effectiveness for the intended use. For example, iodine is a good, low-hazard disinfectant but is inactivated by residual organic matter and by sunlight; quicklime is caustic, can destroy organic debris and germs and is usable on carcasses under wet conditions, but is very hazardous. Proper disinfection steps: disinfect only clean surfaces — dirty surfaces or those with significant organic matter must be cleaned first; physically remove organic matter (soil, manure, straw, feed); soak, wash with soap and brush, rinse, and dry before applying disinfectant; use the correct dosage/concentration for the product; prepare enough volume for the surface area being treated; and use proper equipment — a sprayer gives good contact between fine disinfectant droplets and the surface. Warning: all disinfectants are toxic and hazardous in concentrated (undiluted) form.
